## Problem 1: Simulation

Data Generating Process

I simulate an outcome variable (Y) as a linear function of a treatment variable (X) and a confounding variable (Z), with random error.

```{r}
# Load libraries
library(MASS) 
library(ggplot2)

# Set random seed and sample size
set.seed(123)
n <- 500

# Specify means and variance-covariance matrix
mu <- c(2, 4)

vcov <- matrix(c(1, 0.8, 0.8, 1), 2, 2)

# Generate correlated treatment and confounder
design_mat <- mvrnorm(n, mu = mu, Sigma = vcov)
colnames(design_mat) <- c("X", "Z")

# Generate outcome variable with random error
Y <- -3 + 5*design_mat[,1] + 1.5*design_mat[,2] + rnorm(n)

# Create dataframe
data <- data.frame(
  X = design_mat[,1],
  Z = design_mat[,2],
  Y = Y
)

# Inspect the simulated data
head(data)
```

True Linear Model

```{r}
# Fit the true model
model_true <- lm(Y ~ X + Z, data = data)

# Print regression summary
summary(model_true)
```

### (a) Central Limit Theorem 

```{r}
# Set random seed
set.seed(456)

# Number of simulation
n_sim <- 1000

# Vector to store estimated treatment coefficients
coef_true <- numeric(n_sim)

# Repeat the simulation
for (i in 1:n_sim) {
  
  # Generate correlated X and Z
  design_mat <- mvrnorm(n, mu = mu, Sigma = vcov)
  
  # Generate the outcome variable
  Y <- -3 + 5*design_mat[,1] + 1.5*design_mat[,2] + rnorm(n)
  
  # Create a simulated dataset
  sim_data <- data.frame(
    X = design_mat[,1],
    Z = design_mat[,2],
    Y = Y
  )
  
  # Fit the true model
  model <- lm(Y ~ X + Z, data = sim_data)
  
  # Store the estimated coefficient of X
  coef_true[i] <- coef(model)["X"]
  
}

# Calculate mean and standard deviation
mean(coef_true)
sd(coef_true)

# Create dataframe for plotting
coef_data <- data.frame(coef_true = coef_true)

# Plot the sampling distribution
ggplot(coef_data, aes(x = coef_true)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
                 bins = 30,
                 fill = "lightblue",
                 color = "white") +
  geom_density(color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5,
             color = "red",
             linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Sampling Distribution of Treatment Coefficient",
    x = "Estimated Coefficient of X",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

I generated 1,000 simulated datasets, each containing 500 observations, and estimated the true model for each dataset. The sampling distribution of the treatment coefficient is approximately normal, with a mean of 4.9991 and a standard deviation of 0.0750. The distribution is centered near the true coefficient of 5, consistent with the normality of the OLS estimator under the specified data generating process.


### (b) Bootstrap Standard Error

```{r}
# Set random seed
set.seed(789)

# Number of bootstrap replications
B <- 2000

# Vector to store bootstrap estimates
boot_coef <- numeric(B)

# Bootstrap resampling
for (b in 1:B) {

  # Resample observations with replacement
  boot_data <- data[
    sample(1:nrow(data),
           size = nrow(data),
           replace = TRUE),
  ]

  # Fit the true model
  model_boot <- lm(Y ~ X + Z, data = boot_data)

  # Store the coefficient of X
  boot_coef[b] <- coef(model_boot)["X"]

}

# Calculate bootstrap standard error
boot_se <- sd(boot_coef)

# Extract the original OLS standard error
ols_se <- summary(model_true)$coefficients["X", "Std. Error"]

# Compare standard errors
print(boot_se)
print(ols_se)
```

### (c) Omitted Variable Bias

```{r}
# Fit a model without the confounding variable
model_omitted <- lm(Y ~ X, data = data)
summary(model_omitted)

# Number of simulations
n_sim <- 1000

# Vector to store estimated coefficients
coef_omitted <- numeric(n_sim)

# Repeat the simulation using the omitted model
set.seed(456)

for (i in 1:n_sim) {

  # Generate correlated X and Z
  design_mat <- mvrnorm(n, mu = mu, Sigma = vcov)

  # Generate outcome
  Y <- -3 + 5*design_mat[,1] +
       1.5*design_mat[,2] + rnorm(n)

  # Create simulated dataset
  sim_data <- data.frame(
    X = design_mat[,1],
    Z = design_mat[,2],
    Y = Y
  )

  # Fit the omitted variable model
  model <- lm(Y ~ X, data = sim_data)

  # Store the estimated coefficient of X
  coef_omitted[i] <- coef(model)["X"]

}

# Calculate mean and standard deviation
mean(coef_omitted)
sd(coef_omitted)

# Plot the omitted model's sampling distribution
omitted_data <- data.frame(coef_omitted = coef_omitted)

ggplot(omitted_data, aes(x = coef_omitted)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 30,
    fill = "lightblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_density(color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5,
             color = "red",
             linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Sampling Distribution: Omitted Variable Model",
    x = "Estimated Coefficient of X",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

# Compare with the true model from part (a)
comparison_data <- data.frame(
  coefficient = c(coef_true, coef_omitted),
  model = rep(c("True Model", "Omitted Variable Model"),
              each = n_sim)
)

ggplot(comparison_data,
       aes(x = coefficient, fill = model, color = model)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5,
             linetype = "dashed",
             color = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 6.2,
             linetype = "dotted",
             color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Sampling Distributions: True vs. Omitted Model",
    x = "Estimated Coefficient of X",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

Repeating the simulation 1,000 times produced an approximately normal sampling distribution with a mean of 6.1982 and a standard deviation of 0.0578, compared with 4.9991 and 0.0750 in the true model. 

The omitted-variable model overestimates the true treatment effect of 5 because X and Z are positively correlated, causing the estimated coefficient of X to absorb part of the effect of Z. 

This suggests that an approximately normal sampling distribution and statistical significance do not necessarily imply an unbiased estimate of the true treatment effect.



## Problem 2: Data Analysis

### (a) Difference in Means Hypothesis Test

I examine whether mean net approval differs between country-year
observations with high and low levels of household debt. I divide the observations into two groups based on the sample median of household debt.

The null hypothesis is that the two groups have equal population means, while the alternative hypothesis is that their means differ.

I use a two-sided Welch's t-test with a significance level of 0.05 because the population variances are unknown and the two groups may have unequal variances.

```{r}
# Load libraries
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Load the dataset
toy_data <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/reshi-rajan/Methods-Resources/refs/heads/main/toy_data.csv")

# Create net approval variable
toy_data <- toy_data |>
  mutate(net_approval = approval_not_smoothed -
           disapproval_not_smoothed)

# Inspect the data
head(toy_data)

# Remove observations with missing values
analysis_data <- toy_data |>
  filter(!is.na(hh_debt),
         !is.na(net_approval))

# Calculate median household debt
debt_median <- median(analysis_data$hh_debt)

# Create high- and low-debt groups
analysis_data <- analysis_data |>
  mutate(
    debt_group = if_else(
      hh_debt > debt_median,
      "High",
      "Low"
    ),
    debt_group = factor(
      debt_group,
      levels = c("High", "Low")
    )
  )

# Check group sizes
table(analysis_data$debt_group)

# Calculate descriptive statistics by group
analysis_data |>
  group_by(debt_group) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_approval = mean(net_approval),
    sd_approval = sd(net_approval)
  )

# Conduct Welch's two-sample t-test
test_result <- t.test(
  net_approval ~ debt_group,
  data = analysis_data,
  alternative = "two.sided",
  var.equal = FALSE,
  conf.level = 0.95
)

# Print t-test results
test_result
```

The mean net approval is -3.29 for the high-debt group and -7.15 for the low-debt group, a difference of 3.86 percentage points. However, this difference is not statistically significant (t = 1.19, p = 0.237), so I fail to reject the null hypothesis of equal means. Substantively, the high-debt group has higher net approval on average, but the evidence is insufficient to conclude that the difference exists in the population.


### (b) Linear Regression

```{r}
# Set Low-debt group as the reference category
analysis_data$debt_group <- relevel(
  analysis_data$debt_group,
  ref = "Low"
)

# Fit a linear model
model_b <- lm(net_approval ~ debt_group,
              data = analysis_data)

# Print regression summary
summary(model_b)

# Compare p-values from the t-test and regression
test_result$p.value

summary(model_b)$coefficients[
  "debt_groupHigh", "Pr(>|t|)"
]
```


### (c) Permutation Test

```{r}
# Calculate observed difference in means (High - Low)
observed_diff <- mean(
  analysis_data$net_approval[analysis_data$debt_group == "High"]
) - mean(
  analysis_data$net_approval[analysis_data$debt_group == "Low"]
)

print(observed_diff)

# Set random seed and number of permutations
set.seed(123)
B <- 5000

# Store permutation statistics
perm_diff <- numeric(B)

# Conduct permutation test
for (i in 1:B) {

  # Randomly shuffle group labels
  shuffled_group <- sample(analysis_data$debt_group)

  # Calculate difference in means
  perm_diff[i] <- mean(
    analysis_data$net_approval[shuffled_group == "High"]
  ) - mean(
    analysis_data$net_approval[shuffled_group == "Low"]
  )

}

# Calculate two-sided permutation p-value
perm_p <- (sum(abs(perm_diff) >= abs(observed_diff)) + 1) / (B + 1)

print(perm_p)

# Plot null distribution
perm_data <- data.frame(perm_diff = perm_diff)

ggplot(perm_data, aes(x = perm_diff)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 30,
    fill = "lightblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_density(color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = observed_diff,
    color = "red",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Permutation Null Distribution",
    x = "Difference in Mean Net Approval (High - Low)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

# Compare p-values
p_ttest <- test_result$p.value

p_regression <- summary(model_b)$coefficients[
  "debt_groupHigh", "Pr(>|t|)"
]

p_values <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Welch t-test", "OLS Regression", "Permutation Test"),
  P_value = c(p_ttest, p_regression, perm_p)
)

print(p_values)
```

The permutation null distribution is approximately normal and centered around zero. The observed mean difference of 3.862 falls within the distribution and is not statistically significant (p = 0.234). The permutation p-value is very close to those from the Welch's t-test (p = 0.237) and OLS regression (p = 0.236). All three tests lead to the same conclusion: we fail to reject the null hypothesis of equal means at the 0.05 significance level.
